text.p: Former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev warned U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday not to "flex his muscles" at Russia over NATO expansion during his summit with President Boris Yeltsin.

Gorbachev, visiting Argentina, advised Yeltsin to make it clear to Clinton "he would be laying a minefield under the whole post-Cold War process" if he insists on drawing former Soviet bloc countries into the Western alliance.

Clinton and Yeltsin began a two-day summit on Thursday in Helsinki amid tension about U.S. support for NATO expansion and Russia's vow to defend its interests "like never before." Russia is bitterly opposed to NATO plans to invite new members -- probably Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to join the 16-member alliance at a meeting in Madrid in July.

Gorbachev, who pitched the Soviet Union into a reform process that brought it closer to the West but also led to the breakup of the former Soviet state, told reporters in Buenos Aires: "If Clinton goes to the summit with old preconceptions and tries to flex his muscles and pressure them using old-style methods ... he will look like a president who has not learned from past experiences."

The former president is visiting Argentina as head of the environmental group Green Cross. In an interview with the Argentine newspaper La Nacion he complained of dire levels of poverty in his homeland that could lead to chaos.
"Sixty percent of the Russian population lives in absolute poverty according to official data. We believe the rate is higher and may be as much as 80 percent," he said.
"I don't like saying these things but there are people who have not been paid their wages for six months. There are 22 million people unemployed. That is a very dangerous burden."
The architect of Soviet economic and political reforms also made a plea for Cuba, urging the West to break with Washington's long-standing economic embargo on the communist-ruled island.
"I believe lifting the blockade would give Cuba the chance to launch the democratic process," he said. But he did not recommend that Cuba imitate the reform path he took.
"Cuba should do this the Cuban way, not the Soviet way. There is not one sole model," he said.
